AI development could be a lot more efficient.

We have computers sitting idle while different research teams are tackling similar problems, often without access to each other's findings.

It turns out that @eigencloud has two pretty clever ideas for making better use of both:

→ @DarkbloomAI: A network where Mac owners can put their unused computing power to work by letting developers run AI models on their machines.

Mac owners earn additional income, while developers get access to cheaper computing power.

→ @YukonResearch: A research platform where researchers and AI agents work together to make AI models run faster.

One Yukon challenge from the article showed how much faster an AI model could run on the same hardware, just by improving the software.

Now imagine applying those improvements across Darkbloom's network of Macs. The results could be more AI requests processed, lower costs, and better use of existing hardware.

A win-win in my book.

🚨🇫🇷 France is now borrowing at more than 5% over 10 years and consequences could be far more significant than markets currently anticipate - FT

📈 Despite rising bond yields, France remains far from a sovereign debt crisis but the spread between French and German 10-year bonds is hovering around 170 basis points. Moreover, when we convert five-year sovereign yields into US dollars using cross-currency swaps, stripping out much of the difference in monetary policy expectations, French debt shows a synthetic yield above 6% compared with 5% for the US. Even though, this is not the rate at which France actually borrows, it reveals a significant deterioration in the compensation investors demand to hold French government debt.

💰 With an average debt maturity of more than eight years, France benefits from a substantial buffer as higher interest rates do not immediately affect the entire outstanding debt stock. However, this buffer only delays the problem and doesn't eliminate it. The French government's interest bill is expected to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027. With €340 billion in medium- and long-term bond issuance planned for 2027, net of buybacks, a sustained 100-basis-point increase in borrowing costs could translate into several billion euros in additional annualized interest expenses on new issuance alone. If rates remain elevated long enough, this could structurally weaken France's public finances.

🇪🇺 France's situation remains nowhere near the European sovereign debt crisis of 2011–2012, when Greek bond spreads reached several thousand basis points. However, France doesn't need to experience a Greek-style crisis to suffer a major deterioration in debt sustainability. Unlike the US, whose interest burden as a share of GDP is actually higher, France does not independently control its monetary policy. Some argue that worsening French economic conditions would push the ECB to act but there is no guarantee that a confidence crisis specific to France would trigger monetary easing across the entire eurozone.

⚠️ When borrowing costs remain elevated while economic growth is weak and primary deficits persist, stabilizing public debt requires fiscal adjustments. Those adjustments can themselves weigh on economic growth making fiscal consolidation even harder. France still has full access to capital markets and government bond auctions continue to attract investors but we may face a fiscal credibility crisis that gradually becomes entrenched.

➡️ I believe the main risk is that investors continue to finance France at a price that makes its fiscal trajectory increasingly difficult to sustain, and that doesn't require a spectacular sovereign debt crisis.

*FT link: https://t.co/14FKUfN3nC

#Uranium #Gold #Silver #Copper #Graphene $HGRAF
Sunday thoughts | October 25, 2026

A tough stretch for commodities as oil keeps rising and rate-hike fears return. Gold and silver have been under pressure, while uranium prices have held up better.
Uranium equities are another story. Stocks can get swept up in broader selloffs even when the underlying commodity remains strong.

Then there’s tax-loss selling. I’ve seen it start early several times in recent years. My approach is to trim vulnerable positions around early October and look for opportunities to rebuild by mid-December. That can set up strong returns in the first months of the new year, although the timing never follows a perfect script.

For gold, silver and copper, my near-term conviction is lower.

If oil keeps climbing and central banks respond with higher rates, precious metals could remain under pressure. A sharper economic slowdown would also weigh on copper demand.

But the policy response matters. If growth weakens enough, central banks could become more willing to tolerate inflation and eventually return to easing—potentially including QE. That could improve the backdrop for precious metals. We may be heading toward another attractive entry point for gold and silver over the coming months.

Uranium has a different demand profile.

Operating reactors need fuel through economic cycles. Restarts add demand, and fuel represents a relatively small share of a nuclear plant’s overall costs. Utilities have much less room to cut consumption simply because growth slows.

My thesis remains that the supply shortfall, combined with prices that still don’t justify enough new mine development, creates a strong case for higher uranium prices over time.

My largest investment by far, however, is HydroGraph $HGRAF.

I added heavily during the recent selloff. The latest company update reaffirmed that plans remain on track, and the shares rallied around 30% in a day. That gives you an idea of how much pessimism had been priced in.

The next milestones I’m watching: the upcoming redomiciliation vote, completion of the move, and the first larger purchase orders expected before year-end.

Lately, I find myself looking around my house, at the road outside and at passing vehicles, thinking: how many of these materials could eventually incorporate graphene?

Where ultra-low loadings can deliver lighter weight, greater strength, longer life or lower total costs, the commercial appeal is obvious. 

The flow of graphene news keeps growing. There will be multiple producers and multiple winners. HydroGraph is my strongest bet because HydroGraph produces 99.8% pure carbon content graphene in the most consistent process with the lowest environmental footprint in the industry.

The expextations are contracts this year, followed by a substantial production ramp next year. That’s why I’ve been loading the truck.

As always, this is my own view and positioning. Do your own due diligence.

How to value any token from its cash flows (+ what you need): 👇 

> You need a spreadsheet
> 4 free sites
> A few hours
> Or use my free bot (link at the end)

Where do you get the data?
 > DefiLlama: fees, revenue, holder revenue > CoinGecko: price and supply > The protocol's docs: fee routing, allocation, vesting > The US 10-year yield and Damodaran's country risk table

Step 1: Find holder earnings (E0)
 • Download daily fees, revenue and holders revenue from DefiLlama • Whole days only. Skip today. • E0 = the last 365 days of holders revenue • Under a year: take the lower of the 90-day total and the 14-day total scaled to a year • Under 30 days of history: stop • Only count money that reaches holders • Tokens paid out as new issuance are dilution, not earnings • EPS = E0 ÷ total supply

Step 2: Work out supply
 • Use total outstanding supply, not circulating • Include vested tokens nobody has claimed • If tokens are unissued, check two things: do the team wallets hold the biggest balance, and do fees alone fund operations and buybacks? • Both true: count 60% of the unissued pool (base), 10% (bull), 0% (bear) • Otherwise: 100% (bear), 60% (base), 10% (bull) • Run both versions and compare

Step 3: Build the discount rate (Ke)
 • Add: risk-free rate + equity risk premium (about 4–6%) + regulatory + governance + alignment + smart-contract risk • Alignment: 0% automatic, 1% changeable, 2% decided case by case • Smart-contract risk: about 2% after a big exploit, about 0.5% if battle-tested • Under 90 days old: add up to 2 points • Long-run rate: same layers, smart-contract risk at its floor

Step 4: Choose 7 years of growth
 • Take the category's trailing fee growth from DefiLlama • Base = a third of that, capped at 20% a year • Bull = +10 points, bear = −10 points • Category down sharply from its peak? Start from the lower level • Structural decline: base growth 0%
Step 5: Estimate the exit multiple • Judge the moat and pick a return on equity (ROE): 20% for weak, 100%+ for strong • No moat: ROE = long-run Ke • Long-run growth (gT): 3.0% bear, 3.5% base, 4.5% bull • P/E = (1 − gT ÷ ROE) ÷ (long-run Ke − gT)

Step 6: Calculate value per token
 • Grow earnings each year: E(t) = E0 × (1 + g)^t • Divide by that year's supply: add vested or emitted tokens, subtract burned ones • Discount each year by (1 + Ke)^t and add up all 7 • Exit value = P/E × year-7 EPS, discounted back 7 years • Fair value = discounted payouts + discounted exit • Repeat for bear, base and bull, then weight 20/60/20

Step 7: Compare with price
 • Fair value vs today's price, as a % above or below • Break-even growth: change base growth until your value equals the price (goal-seek does this) • That's the growth the market is already pricing in

Step 8: Check yourself
 • Do the three scenarios look sensible together? • Does one changed assumption swing the answer? That input is carrying the result. • Write down every guess you couldn't verify • Rerun with the other emissions setting

Fees not reaching holders yet?
 • Value it twice: once as if nothing reaches holders, once with the fee switch on or buybacks restarted • Weight the second case by your own odds, e.g. 40% within a year if buybacks are only paused
Keep a record • Note every number's source and the date you got it • Label your own judgement calls as yours

If we take the view that power becomes the ultimate bottleneck, the capex optimization constraint shifts to the one input China has in greater abundance vs US (who has relatively more chips)

So the compute forward curve actually becomes an epic industrial duration battle where China competes at the front end and the US holds the long end. The question then becomes who is the dog and who is the tail, and which strategic advantage will roll down the curve faster- chips or power? I think anyone who understands the leverage of depreciation knows the answer.

In other words this is a warning to US policymakers: the long end of the compute curve was never really about contracted chips security. It’s about energized megawatts and that’s basically the one duration the US is shortest vs its biggest geopolitical rival
